questions.question: Air is not a liquid, yet chemists count it as a solution: its gases are spread evenly through one another, as salt is spread through the water of the sea. Every breath a person takes is a small sample of it. Which gas is the solvent in air, and why?
questions.answer: Nitrogen, as there is more of it than any other gas
choices: Nitrogen, as there is more of it than any other gas
Oxygen, as it is the gas that living things breathe
Water vapour, as water is the universal solvent
Carbon dioxide, as it dissolves so well in water
questions.context: The solvent is the substance a solution holds the most of, and air is about 78 percent nitrogen and 21 percent oxygen, so nitrogen is the solvent and oxygen, water vapour, argon and carbon dioxide are solutes spread through it. Water is the solvent in seawater because seawater is mostly water, but air holds only a little water vapour. A solution need not be a liquid at all: brass is a solid one, with zinc spread through copper.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade names the solute and solvent of a solution and shows that solutions can be gases, with air as the usual example.

questions.question: Water holds salt in the sea and oxygen in a pond, and in the blood it carries nutrients round the body. It dissolves so many substances that chemists call it the universal solvent. What makes water so good at dissolving?
questions.answer: Its molecules have slightly charged ends
choices: Its molecules have slightly charged ends
Its molecules are smaller than all others
It reacts with each thing it touches
It is the only liquid that dissolves solids
questions.context: A water molecule's oxygen end carries a slight negative charge and its hydrogen ends a slight positive one, so water tugs on charged particles, such as the sodium and chloride in salt, and pulls them apart into the water. Dissolving makes no new substance, and water is not the only solvent: alcohol dissolves the iodine in the tincture put on cuts. A hydrogen molecule is smaller than a water molecule, so size is not the reason.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade calls water the universal solvent and explains it by the slight charges on the ends of its molecule.

questions.question: When the tide goes out, a rock pool is left cut off from the sea, full of ordinary seawater. All through a hot, sunny afternoon, much of the water in the pool evaporates. What happens to the concentration of salt in the pool?
questions.answer: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
choices: It rises, as the same salt is in less water
It falls, as the salt goes off with the water
It stays the same, as no salt has been added
It falls, as the Sun's heat breaks the salt down
questions.context: Concentration is how much solute a given amount of solution holds. Evaporation takes away only water, so the salt left behind is crowded into less of it: seawater holds about 35 grams of salt in each kilogram, and a sun-baked rock pool can reach 50 or more. Rain does the opposite, diluting the pool with fresh water.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade defines concentration as the amount of solute in a given amount of solution and asks how it changes when solvent is lost or added.

questions.question: A chemist makes a deep purple solution of potassium permanganate. She measures 10 millilitres of it into a flask and adds 90 millilitres of water, and the liquid turns a pale pink. How much permanganate does the flask hold now, compared with the 10 millilitres she poured in?
questions.answer: The same amount, spread through more water
choices: The same amount, spread through more water
A tenth as much, as the colour is so pale
Ten times as much, as there is more liquid
Less, as some has settled to the bottom
questions.context: Diluting adds solvent and leaves the solute alone: every bit of permanganate she poured is still in the flask, spread through ten times as much liquid, so its concentration is a tenth of what it was and the colour fades. A solute dissolved evenly does not settle, however long the flask stands.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards describe dilution as adding solvent, which lowers the concentration while the amount of solute stays the same.

questions.question: A geologist drops a fist-sized lump of rock salt, the mineral halite, into a beaker of water. Into a second beaker of the same water she drops the same mass of rock salt, crushed to small grains. Neither beaker is stirred. Which salt is gone first, and why?
questions.answer: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
choices: The grains, as more of their surface meets the water
The lump, as its weight drags it down through the water
Both at once, as each holds the same mass of salt
The lump, as water seeps deep into its many cracks
questions.context: Water can only work on a solid where it touches it. Crushing the lump bares far more surface to the water, so the grains dissolve much faster; the lump holds the same mass of salt, but most of it is hidden inside, away from the water.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to predict and explain how surface area changes how fast a solid dissolves.

questions.question: A student drops a blue crystal of copper sulfate into a beaker of cold water and an identical crystal into a beaker of hot water. She stirs neither one. The crystal in the hot water is gone long before the other. Why does the hotter water dissolve it faster?
questions.answer: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
choices: Its particles move faster and strike the crystal more often
Its heat melts the crystal into a blue liquid first
Its heat turns the crystal into a new substance
Its particles grow bigger and push the crystal apart
questions.context: Heating water gives its particles more energy, so they move faster, strike the crystal more often and carry its particles off sooner. The crystal dissolves rather than melts, no new substance forms, and the water's particles stay the same size however hot it gets.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask students to explain, with particles, why a solid dissolves faster in warmer water.

questions.question: A student pours equal scoops of Epsom salt, the crystals used in soaks for sore muscles, into two beakers of warm water. She stirs one beaker and leaves the other still, and the stirred salt is gone far sooner. Why does stirring speed up the dissolving?
questions.answer: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
choices: It keeps bringing fresh water to the crystals
It splits the salt's particles into smaller bits
It lets the water hold more of the salt in all
It mixes in air, and the air dissolves the salt
questions.context: The water right next to a crystal soon fills with dissolved salt and takes in more only slowly; stirring sweeps it away and brings fresh water up against the crystal. Stirring changes how fast the salt dissolves, not how much the water can hold, and no particle is split.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade standards ask why agitation, stirring or shaking, speeds up dissolving.

questions.question: A student stirs spoonful after spoonful of potassium nitrate, a white salt, into a beaker of water at room temperature. At last some crystals stay on the bottom, because the solution is saturated. Which change will get more of those crystals to dissolve?
questions.answer: Warming the water in the beaker
choices: Warming the water in the beaker
Stirring the water much faster
Crushing the crystals to a powder
Leaving the beaker to stand for days
questions.context: A saturated solution holds all the solute it can at its temperature, and stirring, crushing or waiting only make a solid dissolve faster, never make room for more. Warmer water holds more of most solids, and potassium nitrate is a strong case: water near boiling holds more than seven times as much as water at 20 degrees Celsius.
questions.grade_note: Seventh grade teaches the saturated solution and that temperature, unlike stirring or crushing, changes how much of a solid can dissolve.

questions.question: The fish in a pond breathe oxygen gas that is dissolved in its water. Over a long, hot summer the pond warms from 20 to 30 degrees Celsius. How does the amount of oxygen the water can hold change?
questions.answer: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
choices: It falls, as warm water holds less gas
It rises, as warm water dissolves more
It stays the same, as only solids change
It drops to none, as the gas boils away
questions.context: Unlike most solids, gases dissolve less in warmer water, because heat helps their particles escape it: fresh water at 20 degrees Celsius can hold about 9 milligrams of oxygen in a litre, but at 30 degrees only about 7.6. That is why hot, calm summer weather can leave pond fish short of oxygen, while cold, tumbling streams hold plenty.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade solutions units contrast solids with gases, which dissolve less in warmer water, and use the oxygen fish breathe as the example.

questions.question: At a bottling plant, carbon dioxide is forced into chilled water under pressure and each bottle is capped tight. On the shelf the water looks still, with no bubbles in it. When a cap is twisted off, bubbles stream up through the water. Why do the bubbles appear?
questions.answer: The pressure drops, so less gas can stay dissolved
choices: The pressure drops, so less gas can stay dissolved
The pressure drops, so the water starts to boil
Air rushes in and reacts with the water to make gas
Air rushes in and forms the bubbles in the water
questions.context: The more pressure a gas is under, the more of it a liquid can hold, so the tight cap keeps extra carbon dioxide dissolved. Opening the bottle drops the pressure to that of ordinary air, and the carbon dioxide the water can no longer keep comes out as bubbles; the water is far too cold to boil.
questions.grade_note: Seventh-grade solutions units use fizzy water to show a gas dissolved in a liquid, which comes out of solution when the pressure drops.
